papers.title: Hidden Drowsiness in Wakefulness: Differences in Resting-State EEG Profiles in Natural Short Sleepers Versus Recommended Length Sleepers.
papers.abstract: Chronic insufficient sleep affects cardiovascular, endocrine, immune and nervous systems and is linked to cognitive decline and increased mortality. Among habitual short sleepers, a subgroup known as natural short sleepers (NSS) report sleeping ≤ 6 h per night without experiencing subjective daytime dysfunction. However, discrepancies between subjective and objective markers of alertness raise questions about their true cognitive state. NSS have been described as high in behavioural activation, a phenotype overlapping with ADHD and mania in which dysregulation of resting-state brain arousal has been well documented. Despite these parallels, few studies have investigated the neurophysiological features of NSS. The current study examined resting-state EEG in NSS and recommended-length sleepers (RLS) during eyes-open conditions. Results showed that NSS exhibited significantly higher global alpha power and regionally steeper aperiodic exponents, particularly in occipital areas, both markers of increased drowsiness. Although global exponent values did not differ significantly, a significant Group × Region interaction was observed and NSS showed a trend toward increasing aperiodic exponents over time, suggesting less stable wakefulness under low-stimulation conditions. These findings point to subtle neurophysiological differences in NSS, raising the possibility that their perceived resilience to short sleep may mask underlying drowsiness.

These markers suggest increased drowsiness and less stable wakefulness under low stimulation, possibly masked by perceived resilience to short sleep.

papers.title: Targeting memory consolidation in major depression via pharmacological slow-wave sleep promotion
papers.abstract: Slow-wave sleep (SWS) has been implicated in memory consolidation and brain plasticity and proposed as a therapeutic target in major depressive disorder (MDD). However, whether pharmacological promotion of SWS causally improves memory consolidation remains unknown. Gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), a robust enhancer of SWS, represents a promising drug-repurposing candidate to target this pathway. We therefore conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 22 patients with MDD and 20 matched healthy controls receiving single nocturnal doses of GHB, trazodone as an active comparator, or placebo under polysomnographic monitoring (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04082806). Declarative, procedural and emotional memory were assessed before and after sleep. GHB strongly increased SWS duration and delta power, whereas trazodone produced smaller changes in sleep-stage composition. Contrary to our hypothesis, neither drug improved memory consolidation across domains. Exploratory analyses revealed weak associations between global sleep-stage measures and memory, alongside selective associations with spindle and spectral features. These findings challenge the assumption that increasing SWS alone is sufficient to improve overnight memory consolidation and suggest that more targeted modulation of sleep oscillatory dynamics may be required.

papers.title: MLE EEG Toolbox: A Personal AI Laboratory Assistant for Literature-Informed and Reproducible M/EEG Research
papers.abstract: Electrophysiological research increasingly relies on complex analytical workflows, yet integrating methodological evidence, computational execution and reproducibility remains challenging. Here we introduce MLE EEG Toolbox, a framework for building a personal AI laboratory assistant for electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) research. The toolbox integrates locally deployed AI, natural-language-guided analysis, literature retrieval and methodological comparison, and reproducible computational workflows. A constrained language model translates research instructions into validated, researcher-approved operations, while literature-informed guidance supports parameter selection and protocol reconstruction. Computational provenance enables transparent inspection and replay of analytical workflows. The assistant achieved action-selection accuracies of 85.6% for EEG and 95.5% for MEG, while 142 cross-platform tests demonstrated close numerical agreement. Applications to public EEG and MEG datasets illustrated integrated spectral, network, decoding and source analyses. Running on standard personal computers without external AI APIs or token charges, MLE EEG Toolbox provides an accessible, researcher-controlled environment that connects methodological knowledge with reproducible electrophysiological analysis.

papers.title: A Soft Sponge-Pillar Electrode Platform for Motion-Tolerant Ambulatory EEG and Sleep Monitoring.
papers.abstract: Long-term wearable electrophysiological recording systems are essential for both clinical and real-world environments. While a wide range of wearable devices have been reported for electrocardiogram (ECG) and electromyogram (EMG) recording applications, most electroencephalography (EEG) measurements still require subjects to remain stationary while wearing rigid and uncomfortable equipment. Here, a soft and wearable sponge pillar EEG electrode is presented for long-term and motion-tolerant EEG recording. The electrode is composed of two layers of a carbon black (CB)-polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) composite, where a firmer solid base assists in bypassing hair, enabling stable access to the scalp, while a porous sponge tip ensures comfort, reliable contact, and low skin-electrode impedance. Fabricated via a sugar templating process without microfabrication steps, the microporous sponge structure offers low modulus and significantly enhances the contact area with the skin when loaded with conductive gel. This allows the electrode to achieve a lower contact impedance of $1.62 \times 10^{4}\,Ω$ at 10 Hz, outperforming conventional gelled electrodes while maintaining gel stability for over 18 hours. With the electrodes integrated into wearable form factors such as headbands, headphones, and baseball caps, EEG signal recording during motion have been demonstrated, achieving a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 16.46 dB. These features establish the sponge pillar electrode as a promising platform for next generation wearable EEG systems, enabling comfortable, stable, and prolonged brain signal acquisition on ambulatory subjects and in naturalistic environments.

papers.title: Protocol-aware dual-view single-channel EEG sleep staging with improved N1 discrimination on public sleep-EDF and SHHS benchmarks.
papers.abstract: To develop and evaluate DualViewSeqSleepNet, a protocol-aware single-channel EEG model for automatic sleep staging under reproducible public benchmark settings. The model integrates raw-waveform and spectral encoders, gated epoch-level fusion, lightweight bidirectional cross-epoch aggregation, and an auxiliary loss targeting Wake-N1 and N1-N2 transitions. Primary testing used the exact Sleep-EDF SC-subset protocol of SeriesSleepNet. Secondary no-retuning evaluation used SHHS-1 healthy C4-A1 data. On Sleep-EDF, DualViewSeqSleepNet achieved macro-F1 0.821, accuracy 0.869, and Cohen's kappa 0.808, exceeding the SeriesSleepNet anchor and improving N1 F1 from 0.506 to 0.535. On SHHS-1, it reached macro-F1 0.791 and accuracy 0.854 without architecture-family retuning. Ablation and robustness analyses supported the contributions of dual-view fusion, cross-epoch aggregation, and N1-aware supervision. DualViewSeqSleepNet provides a modest, protocol-aligned improvement for public single-channel sleep staging, especially near Wake-N1-N2 boundaries, but does not establish external clinical validation or autonomous deployment readiness.

papers.title: Circadian feeding rhythm loss drives sex-specific β-cell dysfunction in diet-induced obesity.
papers.abstract: Diet-induced obesity (DIO), modeled by a high-fat diet (HFD), adversely affects circadian glucose homeostasis partly by dysregulating fasting/feeding cycles. However, its impact on circadian β-cell function and relevant transcriptional programs remains unclear. To investigate this, we exposed male and female C57BL/6 mice to either chow or HFD for eight weeks and assessed behavioral (feeding/activity), physiological (glucose tolerance/insulin secretion), transcriptomic (RNA sequencing (RNA-seq)), and epigenomic (Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin using Sequencing (ATAC-seq)) circadian rhythms. Additionally, we tested whether normalizing fasting/feeding cycles via time-restricted feeding (tRF) during the dark- or light-phase of the circadian cycle could mitigate DIO's deleterious effects. DIO disrupted circadian fasting/feeding rhythms, with greater disruption in males than females (p<0.05 vs. CHOW). In males, DIO abolished circadian regulation of glucose tolerance and in vivo glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) (p<0.05 vs. chow), whereas female mice maintained circadian glucose homeostasis. RNA-seq analysis of male islets revealed a 42.1% reduction in circadian-regulated transcripts under DIO, with weakened rhythms in key β-cell pathways such as insulin secretion. Moreover, ATAC-Seq analysis indicated reduced chromatin accessibility of genes/pathways related to insulin secretion and glucose hemostasis under DIO (p<0.05 vs. chow) during both dark- or light-phase of the circadian cycle. Notably, dark-phase time-restricted feeding (tRF) restored circadian glucose tolerance, GSIS, and islet gene expression, whereas light-phase tRF enhanced β-cell function during the normally inactive/light phase of the circadian cycle, further suppressing circadian rhythmicity of the islet transcriptome. Motif analysis indicated that DIO suppressed the activity of D-box transcription factors (TFs) (DBP and TEF) while enhancing the activity of ETS family TFs (ELK1, ETS2, ELF2, and GABPA), which was partly mitigated by dark-phase tRF. Our study demonstrates that DIO disrupts circadian β-cell function and gene expression by dysregulating fasting/feeding cycles in male mice and reveals significant sex differences in how DIO affects circadian glucose homeostasis and β-cell function.

papers.title: Actimetry-Derived Sleep and Circadian Parameters in a Population-Based Sample from São Paulo: Findings from the EPISONO Cohort.
papers.abstract: To set benchmarks for sleep estimates and for parameters of rest-activity, light exposure, and skin temperature rhythms in a cohort from São Paulo. The present study used data from the 4th edition of the São Paulo Epidemiologic Sleep Study (Estudo Epidemiológico do Sono da cidade de São Paulo, EPISONO, in Portuguese), conducted between 2018 and 2019 ( N = 769). A subset of 404 participants (60% female; mean age: 49.42 ± 14.90 years) was selected based on standardized 7-day records (5 weekdays and 2 free days). Sleep estimates, cosine-based and nonparametric parameters, were extracted and added as dependent variables in generalized linear models to investigate the effects of age, sex, body mass index, socioeconomic status, season of data collection and daylight-saving time on it. Participants aged 40 years or older had earlier sleep, circadian and light exposure timing, and reduced activity levels and amplitude. Females slept longer than males and exhibited a more stable and less fragmented rest-activity rhythm but displayed impaired patterns of exposure to light. Lower socioeconomic status was associated with poorer sleep quality yet less disrupted rhythms. Obesity was correlated with greater instability in the rest-activity rhythm. Seasonal differences revealed that sleep was shorter and later in the spring compared with winter. Our results established reference values for actimetry parameters in the largest city in Latin America and can be applied to similar urban populations. They also highlight vulnerable subgroups with impaired sleep and circadian patterns in this understudied context. These findings can inform public health policies and guide the design of personalized interventions.

papers.title: Spikes in the night: rapid eye movement sleep maximally attenuates epileptiform spike morphology.
papers.abstract: To characterize morphological differences in interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs) across sleep-wake states (rapid eye movement (REM), Non-REM1-3, wakefulness). Prospectively analyzed 7379 IEDs from 17 adults with focal epilepsy (12 unifocal, 5 multifocal) admitted to an epilepsy monitoring unit for continuous surface video-EEG telemetry (41.8±17.2 years, 52.9% females) using custom-developed software allowing manual confirmation of IEDs and sleep-wake states. Nine morphological IED features reflecting paroxysmal depolarizing shift dynamics and magnitude were quantified across three EEG montages (raw, referential and Laplacian). Nonparametric Kruskal-Wallis and post hoc Dunn-Sidak tests with Bonferroni correction assessed state-dependent differences. Only features surviving correction across all montages were considered reproducibly significant. IED morphology varied significantly by state (p < 10-12-10-134). Across all montages and subgroups, REM IEDs had shallowest slopes (upslope 2.91-4.22 μV/s; downslope 2.87-4.33 μV/s), bluntest peaks (27.04°-40.24°), and shortest amplitudes and smallest area, (multifocal-driven). Awake IEDs had steepest slopes (upslope 8.97-15.23 μV/s; downslope 7.54-13.84 μV/s), and spikiest peaks (8.18°-14.44°). NREM IEDs were intermediate. Epileptiform morphology in REM was most attenuated. Shallower slopes, blunter peaks, shorter, and smaller-area IEDs indicate an electrobiological milieu less promoting of epileptic activity than NREM's synchronized state or wakefulness's maximally responsive state. Despite REM and wakefulness being desynchronized on surface EEG, REM's morphological IED divergence raises future directions into sui generis anti-epileptic mechanisms, including network connectivity and pH-responsive orexinergic glial dynamics. The sleep-wake cycle strongly modulates epileptic activity, yet seizures rarely arise from REM (~1%). However, REM contains sufficient IEDs to characterize morphology and probe potential anti-epileptic solutions via their underlying cellular mechanisms.

papers.title: NeuroSim: a clinically informed multi-disorder EEG simulator with personalized pattern injection and AI-driven neurological modeling
papers.abstract: Deep learning for electroencephalography (EEG) based neurodiagnostics is constrained by the limited availability of labeled clinical recordings. Datasets covering Alzheimers disease (AD), Parkinsons disease (PD), schizophrenia (SCZ), epilepsy (EPI), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are scarce, demographically narrow, and heterogeneous across acquisition sites, while privacy requirements restrict data sharing. Existing EEG simulators typically address a single disorder or trade biological interpretability for statistical fidelity. This study presents NeuroSim, a simulation framework that generates synthetic multichannel EEG with user-controlled injection of disease-specific patterns across five disorders and multiple severity levels. A physiologically motivated baseline generator produces band-limited rhythms, event-related potentials, artifacts, and hierarchical subject-level and trial-level variability. Disease patterns are introduced through region-specific and severity-specific spectral modulation that encodes established biomarkers, including posterior alpha suppression in AD, motor beta enhancement in PD, and spike-wave discharges in EPI. An interactive interface exposes montage, sampling rate, duration, artifacts, stimuli, affected regions, and severity, and exports signals with reproducible metadata. The simulated signals reproduced the expected biomarker directionality under spectral, topographic, and multivariate statistical analysis. A convolutional-attention classifier trained on simulated data reached 95.3 to 96.8 percent hold-out accuracy, and post hoc explainability analyses produced class-separable embeddings with attributions concentrated on pathophysiologically expected electrodes. Application of the analysis pipeline to recordings from the Temple University Hospital EEG Corpus confirmed compatibility with heterogeneous clinical data. In subject-level augmentation experiments on real clinical EEG, supplementing real training data with NeuroSim samples increased classification accuracy from 91.6 to 94.5 percent for AD versus healthy controls and from 90.9 to 94.0 percent for PD versus healthy controls, exceeding the improvement obtained with conventional signal-level augmentation. NeuroSim is released as open-source software to support augmentation, benchmarking, and explainable artificial intelligence in neurological diagnostics.

papers.title: Dopamine dynamics in a mouse model of temporal lobe seizures with impaired consciousness.
papers.abstract: Focal temporal lobe seizures often lead to impaired consciousness. Recent work has shown depressed cortical arousal, with slow waves and decreased cortical acetylcholine as a possible mechanism for impaired consciousness in focal seizures. However, the role of other key subcortical arousal systems such as dopamine is largely unknown. We aimed to address this gap by investigating dopamine dynamics in a mouse model of focal limbic seizures with impaired behavioral responsiveness. We induced focal limbic seizures by brief electrical hippocampal stimulation in awake head-fixed mice with hippocampal and cortical local field potential recordings. Behavior was assessed by a conditioned auditory response task. We measured cortical dopamine with a genetically encoded fluorescent sensor via fiber photometry. Activity of dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) was recorded by calcium measurements. Focal hippocampal seizures were associated with altered cortical electrophysiological activity and impaired behavioral responsiveness. During seizures, we found sustained increases in dopamine in both medial prefrontal and orbital frontal cortex. We also found increased dopaminergic neuronal activity in the VTA during seizures. Despite these sustained increases, transient task-evoked dopaminergic increases in both cortex and VTA were reduced during seizures. Behavioral responses during seizures were reduced, and auditory stimuli without behavioral responses elicited smaller transient VTA dopaminergic signals compared to stimuli with preserved responses. Together, those results reveal distinct dysregulation of dopamine dynamics across sustained and fast time scales during focal limbic seizures. The sustained increases in dopamine suggest that the altered cortical function and impaired consciousness in focal limbic seizures may more closely resemble encephalopathy or delirium than deep sleep. Depressed transient dopamine release with sensory stimuli could also contribute to impaired behavioral responsiveness during seizures. Further work on the role of dopamine could have important therapeutic implications for altered cognition and behavior in people with epilepsy.

papers.title: Seizure Prediction Using Channel-Optimized Intracranial EEG With Variable Interictal and Preictal Durations.
papers.abstract: Objective: Predicting epileptic seizures using electroencephalogram (EEG) signals can provide a critical window for intervention to suppress impending seizures. However, the impact of varying interictal and preictal durations on seizure prediction remains unclear and warrants further exploration. Considering this, this study focuses on seizure prediction using intracranial EEG (iEEG) signals with variable interictal and preictal durations. Method: In this work, we discuss six pairwise combinations in total, involving two interictal durations (24 h and 48 h) and three preictal durations (30 min, 60 min and 90 min), during seizure prediction analysis. Furthermore, we also compare three classification strategies: the all-channel strategy (Strategy 1), the single-channel-based majority voting strategy (Strategy 2) and the channel-optimization-based majority voting strategy (Strategy 3), across each pairwise combination. Results: The long-term SWEC-ETHZ iEEG dataset is utilized to evaluate our method. The results reveal that our method achieves up to 87.7 sensitivity, 94.6 specificity, 92.8 accuracy, 0.912 Area Under the Curve (AUC) and 0.858 F1-score at the segment-based level, along with 95.9 sensitivity and 0.05/h false prediction rate (FPR) at the event-based level. Moreover, the overall performance of Strategy 3 surpasses that of Strategies 1 and 2 in each pairwise combination, indicating that channel optimization is beneficial for improving seizure prediction performance. Conclusion: This work shows high effectiveness in predicting seizures using iEEG signals, with the ability to forecast upcoming epileptic events up to 90 min in advance across both 24-h and 48-h interictal durations.

papers.title: AI-Based Monitoring Devices for the Identification of Circadian Parameters as Digital Predictive Biomarkers of Neurodegenerative Diseases in Older Adults: Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, and related dementias are a growing health burden among older adults. Circadian disruption is increasingly recognized as both a consequence and a potential early marker of neurodegenerative progression. Wearable sensing combined with AI enables continuous, noninvasive, and ecologically valid monitoring of circadian parameters as potential digital biomarkers. This systematic review synthesizes evidence on AI-enhanced wearable and objective sensing devices used to monitor circadian parameters in older and cognitively vulnerable adults and evaluates their potential as digital predictive biomarkers for neurodegenerative diseases. Following PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines, an original search of PubMed, Scopus, and JMIR journals (June 2025) yielded 12 studies, 7 of which met updated eligibility criteria on rescreening. A complementary search of PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library (March 24, 2026) added 3 eligible studies and 3 sensitivity references (excluded records retained to delimit the corpus boundary). Two reviewers (JMH-Z and JM-R) independently assessed risk of bias with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Heterogeneous end points precluded meta-analysis; the narrative synthesis covered 4 prespecified domains: device class, circadian construct, AI and machine learning (ML) method family, and population and neurocognitive context. The final corpus comprised 13 records (10 eligible studies and 3 sensitivity references) published from 2015 to 2025. Wrist actigraphy predominated, and samples ranged from community-dwelling older adults to nursing home residents with advanced dementia (n=16-7297). Circadian parameters included interdaily stability, intradaily variability, relative amplitude, midline estimating statistic of rhythm, acrophase, and circadian stimulus. AI/ML methods included supervised learning (random forests, gradient boosting, and regression models), unsupervised clustering, and algorithm development or validation; 7 studies applied deterministic algorithms without fitting a predictive model. Circadian fragmentation was associated with functional decline, dementia risk, and cognitive performance. Most studies were descriptive or observational with small, nondiverse samples; no AI model was externally validated, and no study followed an AI-specific reporting guideline. AI-enhanced wearable devices show meaningful potential for noninvasive measurement of circadian disruption in older and cognitively vulnerable populations. Evidence certainty is moderate for actigraphy-derived fragmentation-function associations in institutional settings and low for predictive biomarker claims in community populations. From 6 recurring challenges along the sensing-to-biomarker pipeline, we propose a 4-layer reference architecture (sensing and acquisition, circadian parameter extraction, AI/ML inference, and a clinical and validation interface) with a layered validation pathway. Longitudinal, multisite validation studies using standardized circadian metrics, diverse populations, and explainable AI remain necessary before clinical deployment as neurodegenerative biomarkers.

Circadian fragmentation was associated with functional decline, dementia risk, and cognitive performance, but no AI model was externally validated; certainty was moderate for actigraphy-fragmentation associations in institutional settings and low for community predictive biomarker claims, and a 4-layer reference architecture with a layered validation pathway was proposed.

papers.title: Effects of Environmental Enrichment on the Behavior of Scarlet Macaws (Ara macao cyanopterus) for Reintroduction.
papers.abstract: Due to the progressive decline of parrots and macaws (psittacids) worldwide, reintroduction has become an increasingly utilized strategy to restore their wild populations. However, captivity can limit or affect their behaviors, so it is crucial to use techniques that maintain and increase the species-typical behaviors, and the skills needed to survive in the wild. Nevertheless, there are no preparation or identification guides for potential release candidates. We studied the effects of environmental enrichment (EE) on the necessary behaviors for surviving in the wild and the abnormal behaviors of a group of hand reared scarlet macaws (Ara macao cyanopterus) in pre-release phase during pre-enrichment and enrichment phases. Using the Wilcoxon rank test, we evaluated behavioral differences between enrichment phases and used an association index to measure the degree of affiliation between individuals. Additionally, we assigned individual release suitability scores based on comparing released and pre-released activity budgets to identify release candidates. The enrichment phase showed a significant increase in exploration behaviors, a significant decrease in resting, self-care, and abnormal behaviors, greater group cohesion, and a higher number of individuals with high release suitability scores. This phase showed no difference in flight behavior. In conclusion, EE increased the frequency of some beneficial behaviors (such as social interaction, and exploration) and well-being (by reducing abnormal behaviors). Accordingly, EE can be complemented by using quantifiable methods to assess the behavior of individuals for reintroduction.

papers.title: Effects of Circadian Disruption and Chronotype on Postural Stability During Quiet Stance.
papers.abstract: Postural control is fundamental for daily activities and is known to be sensitive to disruptions of the circadian system. The present study investigated how individual circadian alignment influences postural stability in healthy adults. In total, 39 participants wore actigraphs for 2 weeks to obtain circadian regularity and misalignment parameters: composite phase deviation (CPD), interdaily stability (IS), and intradaily variability (IV). Chronotype was assessed from corrected midsleep time on free days. Postural stability was evaluated through center of pressure (COP) trajectories recorded while the participant stood on a force platform under different sensory conditions. Postural dynamics were analyzed using both linear sway measures and recurrence quantification analysis, with particular focus on laminarity (LAM) and trapping time (TT) as indicators of postural control stability and adaptability. Higher circadian disruption, reflected by increased CPD and reduced IS, was associated with greater postural instability, characterized by increased sway magnitude and higher values of LAM and TT, suggesting more intermittent and less adaptive postural control strategies. Additionally, individuals with later chronotypes exhibited poorer postural stability compared with those with earlier chronotypes. Therefore, these findings indicate that circadian disruption is associated with alterations in postural control dynamics, potentially reducing the adaptability of the postural system. Even in healthy adults, irregular sleep-wake patterns may place the sensorimotor system in a suboptimal state, increasing vulnerability to balance impairments.

papers.title: Frontal Low-Frequency Electroencephalographic Coherence in Bipolar Disorder: A Covariate-Controlled Secondary Analysis of a Public Resting-State EEG Feature Dataset.
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo test whether bipolar disorder (BD) is associated with predefined frontal/frontopolar low-frequency scalp electroencephalography (EEG) coherence differences relative to healthy controls (HC), depressive disorder (DD), and schizophrenia (SZ) in a covariate-controlled reanalysis of a public resting-state EEG feature dataset.MethodsThe covariate-complete sample included 472 participants (93 HC, 66 BD, 196 DD, and 117 SZ). Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) models adjusted for age, sex, education, and intelligence quotient (IQ). Primary outcomes were predefined frontal/frontopolar delta, theta, and combined delta-theta coherence means. Electrode-pair, regional, all-frequency, distributional, global-reference, frontopolar, and age sensitivity analyses assessed robustness.ResultsBD had higher adjusted coherence than all comparison groups across the three primary measures (partial η2 = .037-.040); Holm-adjusted BD-HC, BD-DD, and BD-SZ contrasts were significant for each measure. Features surviving false discovery rate correction were concentrated in the delta and theta bands. Findings were robust to distributional, outlier, and global-coherence analyses, but effects were strongest in frontopolar pairs and attenuated as anterior electrodes were excluded.ConclusionsBD showed higher covariate-adjusted frontal/frontopolar low-frequency scalp coherence than HC within this dataset. Differences from DD and SZ were smaller and concentrated in frontopolar pairs susceptible to ocular artifacts. Because only scalp-level coherence features were available and participant-level artifact-rejection data were unavailable, the findings do not establish a diagnostic biomarker, diagnostic specificity, or source-level mechanism. Artifact-controlled replication is required.

papers.title: Dermal α-synuclein seeding in relation to REM sleep behavior disorder across prodromal and Parkinson disease cohorts.
papers.abstract: REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is a well-established prodromal manifestation of synucleinopathy and is closely linked to peripheral clinical features in Parkinson disease (PD). Dermal α-synuclein seed amplification assay (SAA) provides a peripheral measure of pathological α-synuclein across these disease stages. We performed a cross-sectional analysis of data from the Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI), including controls, participants with polysomnography-confirmed RBD, and participants with PD. Skin SAA positivity and participant-level kinetic measures (area under the curve [AUC], maximum fluorescence [Fmax], and time to threshold [TTT]) were assessed at 1:20 and 1:50 lysate dilutions. Participants with PD were further classified as suspected brain/motor-enriched or body/peripheral-enriched based on prespecified exploratory clinical features. Skin SAA positivity was detected in 53.3% of participants with polysomnography-confirmed RBD compared with none of the controls, and RBD participants showed significantly faster amplification than controls at both lysate dilutions. Within PD, binary SAA positivity was higher in the suspected body/peripheral-enriched than brain/motor-enriched phenotype, but the difference was not statistically significant (83.3% vs 47.6%; p = 0.067). All seven kinetic measures were greater in the suspected body/peripheral-enriched phenotype after false discovery rate correction, but these differences were not retained when RBDSQ total score was removed from the classification. RBDSQ total score was the only clinical variable associated with skin SAA kinetics after correction and was significantly associated with six of the seven kinetic measures. These findings show that dermal α-synuclein seeding is detectable in PSG-confirmed prodromal RBD and is associated with RBD-related clinical features within established PD.

papers.title: A scoping review of sleep outcomes in congenital hydrocephalus.
papers.abstract: Congenital hydrocephalus (CH) is associated with long-term neurodevelopmental challenges. Sleep is closely linked to neurodevelopment, cognition, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) dynamics, making it a potentially important but understudied outcome in CH. This scoping review examines the published literature on sleep in patients with CH and identifies priorities for future research. We performed a PRISMA-compliant search across Embase, Ovid MEDLINE, Web of Science, and PsycInfo to identify literature examining the relationship between CH and sleep. Seven studies met inclusion criteria, comprising 1,116 participants across CH and comparison groups. Reported findings included increased total sleep time and sleep apnea burden, greater fatigue relative to normative values, and EEG abnormalities during sleep. Findings were mixed for sleep-related quality of life. Interpretation was limited by small samples, lack of appropriate control groups, inconsistent characterization of CH, variable sleep outcomes, and substantial neurologic comorbidity. Available evidence suggests that some aspects of sleep and sleep-related functioning may be impaired in individuals with CH, but the pattern and prevalence of sleep abnormalities, and the extent to which they are attributable to CH itself, remain uncertain. Larger, controlled studies using well-defined study groups and standardized sleep assessments are needed to better characterize this relationship.

papers.title: Group-specific associations among sleep quality, depressive symptoms, and frontal alpha asymmetry in college students: evidence from a cross-sectional EEG study.
papers.abstract: Poor sleep quality is associated with depressive symptoms, but its accompanying neurophysiological correlates remain unclear in non-clinical college students. This study examined associations among sleep quality, depressive symptoms, and frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA) in students with and without elevated depressive symptoms. This cross-sectional study included 120 college students, comprising 60 students with depressive symptoms (DS) and 60 non-depressed controls (NC), classified using the Self-Rating Depression Scale. Sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and FAA was derived from resting-state EEG. Analyses included BMI-adjusted group comparisons, partial correlations, regression models, and an exploratory indirect-path analysis. False discovery rate correction was applied to multiple comparisons. After BMI adjustment, the DS group had higher PSQI scores [median (P25, P75): 7 (6, 10) vs. 3 (1, 5)] and lower composite FAA values [-0.041 (-0.116, 0.031) vs. 0.056 (0.017, 0.103); both p < 0.001] than the NC group. Similar FAA differences were observed using frontopolar and frontal electrode-pair indices. PSQI scores were positively correlated with depressive symptoms in both groups (DS: r = 0.412, q = 0.006; NC: r = 0.462, q = 0.001). In the DS group, composite FAA was negatively correlated with PSQI (r = -0.322, q = 0.034) and depressive symptoms (r = -0.388, q = 0.010); neither FAA-related association reached statistical significance in the NC group. After BMI adjustment, PSQI and FAA were jointly associated with depressive symptom severity in the DS group (R 2 = 0.243). An exploratory indirect-path analysis yielded an indirect association estimate of 0.092 (95% bootstrap CI: 0.002-0.202). Poorer sleep quality was associated with greater depressive symptom severity in both groups, whereas FAA-related associations were observed mainly in the DS group. These findings suggest that FAA may be a candidate neurophysiological correlate of the concurrent association between sleep quality and depressive symptoms in non-clinical college students. Causal mediation cannot be inferred from this cross-sectional study.

papers.title: Integrated roles of regulatory non-coding RNAs in circadian gene expression and disease pathogenesis.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythm (CR) is an intrinsic biological oscillation of nearly 24 h that does not merely respond to the diurnal cycle of the Earth, but rather actively anticipates it. CR can be disrupted by many environmental, physiological and behavioral factors such as irregular sleep-wake cycles, prolonged exposure to artificial light at night, shift-work schedules, altered feeding schedules, trans meridian travel, aging, psychological stress and neurodegenerative diseases. Disruption of circadian rhythm is associated with the onset of cancer, endocrine disorders, neurological complexities, and metabolic dysfunctions. Advances in RNA biology have highlighted the role of non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) in regulating gene expression related to circadian rhythm. While previous studies mainly reviewed individual ncRNA classes or their roles in specific diseases like cancer, an integrative approach across multiple ncRNA categories and diseases is still elusive. This review summarizes recent progress on the roles of microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, and circular RNAs in circadian rhythm regulation and their dysfunctions that lead to several pathological conditions. Among these transcripts, miRNAs are well-documented post-transcriptional regulators of gene expression, whereas lncRNAs and circRNAs exhibit context-specific gene regulation. Moreover, research on circular RNAs is emerging and warrants more scientific endeavors to unearth their detailed mechanisms. A holistic view of ncRNA-mediated circadian regulation will provide innovative perspectives on disease mechanisms and potentially aid in the development of targeted therapeutics that restore circadian homeostasis.

papers.title: From snoring to obstructive sleep apnea: A narrative review of pathophysiology, clinical implications and multimodal management.
papers.abstract: Snoring is a highly prevalent acoustic phenomenon generated by vibration of the upper airway soft tissues during sleep. Long regarded as a benign social nuisance, it is increasingly recognised as a clinically informative manifestation of upper airway dysfunction. In adults it is still defined almost exclusively by subjective report, since standardised objective acoustic criteria remain unestablished; this definitional weakness explains much of the extreme heterogeneity of prevalence estimates, which range from 2% to 83% across studies. Pathophysiologically, snoring reflects an imbalance between a collapsible pharynx and the mechanisms defending its patency. Framing it within the endotypic model developed for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), collapsibility, muscle responsiveness, arousal threshold and loop gain, clarifies why the snoring-upper airway resistance syndrome-OSA continuum holds for many patients but not for all, and why apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) thresholds capture only part of the clinical picture. We argue that so-called "isolated" snoring may be less inert than assumed: respiratory-effort-related microarousals provide a plausible mechanism for insomnia-like symptoms in a subset of symptomatic snorers, while observational and experimental data suggest potential links between snoring, autonomic activation and cardiometabolic risk. These relationships remain incompletely established, particularly in the absence of documented OSA, and should not be interpreted as evidence of causality. Diagnostic assessment should follow a pre-test probability-based, stepwise logic integrating history, upper airway examination, sleep testing and, in selected patients, drug-induced sleep endoscopy and airflow phenotyping, the latter promising but not yet validated for routine use. Management is correspondingly phenotype-driven. We conclude that the field's central task is the transition of snoring from a self-reported symptom to a measurable physiological trait, a prerequisite for precision-based care and for identifying, among snorers, those in whom further physiological and cardiometabolic evaluation may be warranted.

papers.title: Association between quantitative REM sleep without atonia and skeletal muscle indices by subsequent phenoconversion status in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder.
papers.abstract: To examine whether associations between quantitative REM sleep without atonia (RWA) and skeletal muscle indices differ by subsequent phenoconversion status in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD). This retrospective study included 114 patients with video-polysomnography-confirmed iRBD (88 non-converters, 26 converters). RWA was manually quantified from submental and bilateral tibialis anterior electromyography across all evaluable REM sleep. Tonic RWA index (RWAI) was scored in 30-s epochs according to SINBAR criteria; total RWAI was the percentage of 3-s mini-epochs containing tonic or phasic activity in any channel. Skeletal muscle mass index (SMI; primary outcome) and fat-free mass index (FFMI) were measured by bioelectrical impedance analysis at diagnosis. Linear regression with robust standard errors tested RWAI-by-phenoconversion interactions, adjusting for age, sex, body mass index, apnea-hypopnea index, and regular exercise. Converters had higher tonic, phasic, and total RWAI than non-converters, whereas mean SMI and FFMI were similar. Among converters, total RWAI was inversely correlated with SMI (ρ = -0.61) and FFMI (ρ = -0.54); no such associations were observed among non-converters. In fully adjusted models, the total RWAI-by-phenoconversion interaction was significant for SMI (β = -0.294 per 10 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.513 to -0.076; P = 0.009) and FFMI (β = -0.626; 95% CI, -1.099 to -0.152; P = 0.010). The SMI interaction was robust in most sensitivity analyses. The inverse association between RWA and skeletal muscle indices was more pronounced among patients with iRBD who subsequently phenoconverted. These hypothesis-generating findings require confirmation in larger cohorts.

papers.title: What's in a Story? Studying Neural Narrative Engagement with Auditory Passages Using EEG Inter-Subject Correlation
papers.abstract: Narrative engagement - a state implicating attention as well as emotional and sequential processing - is crucial in contexts ranging from social interaction to education. Yet we still lack an understanding of how narrative contents and listener perceptions relate to the neural responses they elicit. In this study, we investigate relationships between auditory narratives and listener responses using electroencephalography inter-subject correlation (EEG-ISC), a measure of neural synchrony that has been shown to correlate with narrative cohesion, attention, preference, and learning. We analyzed dense-array EEG recorded from 46 adult participants who listened to social and non-social narrated literary excerpts. The data were spatially optimized using Reliable Components Analysis, and ISC was calculated for each of the three maximally reliable components (RCs) on a per-stimulus basis. While we found no significant relationships between EEG-ISC and broad social/non-social categorizations of the excerpts, ISC for high sociocognitive word usage significantly exceeded that of medium and low word usage in the third spatial component, RC3. We further observed a significant positive correlation between participants' summed ratings of interest, compulsion, and enjoyment and ISC, both for RC2 and when summed across RC1-RC3. Interaction analyses suggest that passage content and behavioral responses contributed independently as additive effects to these relationships. Taken together, these findings extend previous research utilizing EEG-ISC in natural speech contexts and, importantly, suggest that the decomposition of EEG into maximally correlated spatial components can separate co-occurring neural processes engaged during story listening.

papers.title: Circadian Regulation of Gastrointestinal Physiology and Disease: Mechanisms, Chrononutrition, and Therapeutic Opportunities.
papers.abstract: Gastrointestinal physiology varies across the 24-h day as central and peripheral clocks coordinate metabolism, epithelial renewal, mucosal immunity, barrier permeability, motility, and microbial activity. Disrupted temporal organization is associated with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, inflammatory bowel disease, colorectal cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma. This narrative review integrates molecular mechanisms with clinical evidence, distinguishing experimental causality from observational associations. Chrononutrition examines interactions between eating patterns and circadian biology, including meal timing, frequency, regularity, and eating-window duration. Human studies support effects of meal timing on peripheral rhythms, but improvements in metabolic markers do not consistently exceed those achieved by calorie restriction. Sleep disturbance predicts disease activity in some inflammatory bowel disease cohorts, whereas preliminary sleep-intervention trials have not established prevention of relapse. Chronomodulated chemotherapy illustrates both potential benefits and implementation barriers, including sex-dependent outcomes and the need for programmable infusion systems. Chronotype, an individual's preference for earlier or later sleep and activity, may modify the feasibility of temporal interventions. Translation requires adequately controlled trials that assess biological phase, disease activity, nutritional safety, adherence, and clinically meaningful outcomes alongside standard care.

papers.title: Clinical outcomes and EEG monitoring in absence epilepsy trials: A narrative review.
papers.abstract: Absence epilepsy is characterized by typical absence seizures with distinct electroclinical signatures. The main semiological feature is sudden behavioral arrest associated with brief impairment of consciousness, and the electroencephalographic (EEG) hallmark pattern is generalized, symmetric 2.5-4 Hz spike-and-wave discharges (GSW). Absence epilepsy diagnosis relies on correlating GSW with observable clinical manifestations. Monitoring therapeutic effects based solely on reported symptoms may be misleading, as behavioral arrest can be difficult to identify. Patients often do not recall most seizures, and observable motor/behavioral signs may be subtle, such as minimal twitches or transient lapses in responsiveness, which may go unnoticed. In clinical trials for absence epilepsies, quantification of GSW activity by EEG offers an objective and accurate measure of electrical burden and therapeutic efficacy. Despite technological limitations, GSW remains a robust neurophysiological endpoint. Increasing evidence indicates that the timing and burden of GSW correlate with epilepsy comorbidities, including attention, cognition, behavior, and sleep. We reviewed the published literature regarding GSW as an outcome measure in absence epilepsy, including nonseizure outcomes and comorbidities. Our review highlights (1) nearly 100% of clinical absence seizures exhibit sustained GSW discharges on EEG; (2) >49% of electrographic seizures are asymptomatic, indicating that reliance on seizure diaries without EEG monitoring underestimates seizure frequency and burden; (3) Genetic Generalized Epilepsy is not a benign condition and is associated with a high prevalence of cognitive and behavioral comorbidities, supporting evaluation beyond clinically observable seizures and the use of prolonged (≥24-h) EEG monitoring; (4) circadian and multidien cycles further emphasize the need for prolonged EEG recordings to reduce timing-related bias; and (5) antiseizure medications effective in absence epilepsy reduce GSW, supporting EEG monitoring as an objective treatment outcome measure. We therefore recommend incorporating ≥24-h EEG in future clinical trials, especially in (young) adults, and exploring comorbidities as important outcome measures. PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: Absence epilepsy causes brief episodes in which a person suddenly stops what they are doing and may not be aware of their surroundings. Many of these seizures have no obvious signs and are often missed or forgotten, meaning seizure diaries alone do not show the full picture. Our review shows that brain recordings (electroencephalographic, EEG), especially when done over 24 h or longer, detect many unrecognized seizures and better measure how well treatments work. EEG findings are also linked to problems with attention, thinking, behavior, and sleep, highlighting the need to look beyond visible seizures when evaluating treatments in clinical trials.

papers.title: Sleep deprivation remodels hepatic immune microenvironment via circadian gene dysregulation and promotes hepatocellular carcinoma progression.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation (SD) is a widespread public health issue that may adversely affect liver health. Although SD is a recognized circadian stressor, the mechanisms linking circadian rhythm-related changes to liver injury remain poorly understood. This study aims to systematically investigate the role of circadian rhythm-related genes (CRGs) in mediating SD-induced remodeling of the liver immune microenvironment and its potential implications for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Transcriptomic datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) following SD. A rat SD model was used to assess hepatic injury via serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST). Functional enrichment analyses and machine learning identified pivotal CRGs. Key genes were validated across datasets and in HCC. Immune infiltration was analyzed using CIBERSORT and the Tumor Immune Estimation Resource (TIMER) database. Experimental validation in a rat SD model demonstrated significant elevations in serum ALT and AST levels, confirming the induction of hepatic injury. SD induced significant alterations in CRGs. CRGs were found to centrally regulate inflammatory, immune, and oncogenic processes. A machine learning framework identified six core CRGs (Cirbp, Srebf1, Fbxo31, Hsp90aa1, Btc, and Dlgap1), whose dysregulated expression was consistently validated. Furthermore, SD led to a significant reshuffling of the hepatic immune landscape, characterized by changes in five distinct immune cell types, which showed strong correlations with the six key CRGs. Notably, among the six hub CRGs, Cirbp and Hsp90aa1 were significantly associated with immune infiltration levels and prognosis in HCC patients. In addition, Serpine1, which was independently identified by LASSO as a key SD-related gene, showed similar associations.

papers.title: Nocturnal Sweating in Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Systematic Review and Exploratory Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is commonly associated with symptoms such as snoring and daytime sleepiness, while atypical manifestations including nocturnal sweating remain less clearly understood. The current systematic review aimed to evaluate the relationship between nocturnal sweating and OSA and to explore possible physiological mechanisms underlying this association. A systematic search identified 10 relevant studies including observational, physiological, and treatment-response investigations. The included studies varied substantially in design, patient characteristics, and methods of assessing nocturnal sweating. Early studies mainly described nocturnal sweating as a nonspecific symptom among OSA patients and failed to demonstrate consistent associations with conventional severity indices such as the apnea-hypopnea index. However, more recent studies have suggested that nocturnal sweating may be associated with hypoxemic burden, rapid eye movement (REM)-related respiratory worsening, sleep fragmentation, and sympathetic nervous system activation rather than respiratory event frequency alone. Physiological studies have demonstrated improvement in sweating after continuous or automatic positive airway pressure therapy, supporting a reversible autonomic mechanism. An exploratory meta-analysis of three comparative studies showed a non-significant increase in nocturnal sweating among OSA patients (odds ratio [OR] = 1.85; 95%CI: 0.87-3.92; I 2 = 91.7%). After exclusion of one study involving untreated moderate-to-severe OSA patients, heterogeneity decreased but the association remained non-significant (OR = 1.31; 95%CI: 0.76-2.23; I 2 = 64.7%). Overall, nocturnal sweating does not appear to represent a specific diagnostic marker of OSA itself, but it may reflect physiological consequences of untreated or severe disease in susceptible individuals.

papers.title: Rituximab-responsive epilepsia partialis continua in autoimmune Polyendocrine syndrome: A video-EEG-EMG polygraphic study.
papers.abstract: Epilepsia partialis continua (EPC) is a rare and challenging form of focal motor status epilepticus. Its occurrence strictly in systemic autoimmune disorders without overt encephalitis is exceptional. Corticosteroids are first-line therapy but may be limited by significant side effects and poor metabolic tolerability. We report a 54-year-old woman with Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome (APS), including autoimmune hepatitis, latent autoimmune diabetes in adults, celiac disease, and hypothyroidism, presenting with continuous jerks of right III-V fingers. Neurological examination showed continuous, irregular jerks confined to the right III, IV, and V fingers. Extensive serum and CSF screenings, including neuronal antibodies, and MRI were unremarkable. Ictal HMPAO-SPECT revealed a focal hyperperfusion in the left hand-knob area of the primary motor cortex. Brain FDG-PET revealed focal hypometabolism in the same region. Video-EEG-EMG polygraphy showed intermittent spikes and polyspikes over the left central region preceding EMG bursts of the right V finger's abductor muscle with a latency of approximately 30-40 ms. These findings were consistent with EPC. Corticosteroids induced marked improvement but were discontinued due to severe glycemic worsening. Subsequent treatment with oral steroids, IVIG, and multiple antiseizure medications were ineffective. Administration of Rituximab led to complete and sustained clinical and electrophysiological remission, which persisted at the 18-month follow-up. EPC can be a severe, focal manifestation of systemic autoimmunity even without encephalitis. Rituximab represents an effective steroid-sparing option for refractory autoimmune EPC, particularly in metabolically vulnerable patients.

papers.title: Metrics Reflecting Cumulative Exposure to Nocturnal Hypoxia Demonstrate Promising Performance in Distinguishing between Moderate and Severe Obstructive Sleep Apnea.

Metrics that quantify integrated hypoxic exposure may provide a more accurate characterization of disease severity. In total, 30 patients with moderate or severe disease were evaluated using actigraphy combined with continuous nocturnal oximetry. papers.title: Depressive symptoms moderate daily anticipated and momentary emotion dynamics and associate with complex brain network topology: Resting-state EEG and ecological momentary assessment evidence.
papers.abstract: The dynamic linkage between anticipated and momentary emotion is a core daily regulatory process, yet the psychopathological and neurophysiological mechanisms disrupting this linkage in depression remain unclear. By bridging macroscopic neural topology with microscopic behavioral dynamics, this study investigated the within-person dynamics of these emotions and their cross-level associations with depressive symptoms and brain network topology. Integrating resting-state electroencephalography (rs-EEG) with a 14-day ecological momentary assessment (EMA; 3 assessments/day), we recruited 96 young adults. Minimum spanning tree (MST) analysis was applied to characterize baseline brain network topology across multiple frequency bands. Dynamic structural equation modeling (DSEM) was employed to examine within-person dynamics and cross-level statistical moderation. Anticipated emotion prospectively predicted subsequent momentary positive emotion (β = .191) and inversely predicted momentary negative emotion (β = -.125). However, baseline depressive symptoms significantly moderated this prospective affective dynamic: Johnson-Neyman analyses identified empirical transition ranges (PHQ-9 scores 5.7-9.7; mild symptom range) beyond which the prospective emotional link attenuated to non-significance. Furthermore, topological metrics in the theta and delta bands exhibited indirect statistical associations with daily emotional dynamics via their cross-sectional relationship with baseline depressive symptoms. An attenuated prospective association between positive anticipation and subsequent momentary emotional experience represents a key affective alteration in depressive distress. This daily emotional attenuation co-occurs with elevated depressive distress and is indirectly associated with a centralized topological organization in low-frequency resting-state brain networks. These findings provide novel neurophysiological indicators and highlight the critical window for ecological interventions before symptom severity reaches the moderate range.

papers.title: Perioperative esketamine is associated with attenuated sleep deprivation-related cognitive dysfunction: a retrospective biomarker cohort study of the ferroptosis-neuroinflammation axis.

Experimental studies increasingly implicate hippocampal ferroptosis, particularly disruption of the SLC7A11-GSH-GPX4 defense axis, in sleep-deprivation-related cognitive injury. Esketamine has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, but whether its perioperative neurocognitive benefit is associated with a ferroptosis-related molecular phenotype in clinical patients remains uncertain. We conducted a retrospective biomarker cohort study of 398 adults aged 60-80 years who underwent elective major non-cardiac surgery between January 2022 and December 2025. Patients were classified according to preoperative sleep deprivation (total sleep time <4 h and sleep efficiency <70% during the night before surgery) and perioperative esketamine exposure, generating four groups: NSD-C, NSD-E, SD-C, and SD-E. The primary outcome was early postoperative cognitive decline on postoperative day (POD) 7, defined by a ≥1-SD deterioration in a composite neuropsychological Z score. In a biomarker subcohort, plasma 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE), malondialdehyde (MDA), glutathione (GSH), glutathione peroxidase activity, inflammatory cytokines, neuronal injury markers, and PBMC expression of GPX4, SLC7A11, and ACSL4 were analyzed. Confounding was addressed using multivariable models and inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting. Bootstrap mediation models examined a ferroptosis-related redox score and IL-6 as candidate mediators. In the cohort, cognitive decline occurred in 32.5% of sleep-deprived patients without esketamine and 17.7% of sleep-deprived patients exposed to esketamine. After adjustment, esketamine exposure in the sleep-deprivation subgroup was associated with lower odds of cognitive decline (adjusted OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.26-0.92). Sleep deprivation was associated with higher 4-HNE, MDA, ACSL4, IL-6, TNF-α, and NSE and lower GSH, GPX activity, GPX4, and SLC7A11; these abnormalities were attenuated in the esketamine-exposed group. The exploratory ferroptosis-related redox score was independently associated with cognitive decline. Under the specified exploratory mediation model, the estimated total mediated proportion was 54%; this model-based decomposition does not establish causal biological mediation. Perioperative esketamine was associated with less pronounced early postoperative cognitive decline in sleep-deprived patients and a less pronounced peripheral ferroptosis-related/inflammatory phenotype.

papers.title: Pain in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder: Findings from longitudinal and deep-phenotyping cohorts.
papers.abstract: Pain is a common non-motor symptom in Parkinson's disease, yet whether it emerges in the prodromal period and whether it reflects underlying dopaminergic degeneration remains poorly characterized. Our objectives are threefold: to determine whether pain is elevated in polysomnogram-confirmed isolated REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD), whether it predicts phenoconversion to overt synucleinopathy, and whether it is associated with regional dopaminergic deficits. Participants with iRBD (n = 507) and demographically-matched controls (n = 33) enrolled in the North American Prodromal Synucleinopathy (NAPS) Consortium from August 2018 through July 31, 2025 were analyzed. Pain was assessed using MDS-UPDRS item 1.9. Cox proportional hazards models - including a time-varying model incorporating repeated assessments - examined pain as a predictor of phenoconversion. Dopamine transporter (DAT) SPECT imaging was performed in a subset (n = 244), and ordinal logistic regression models evaluated associations between regional striatal binding ratios and pain severity. An independently recruited clinically enriched chronic pain cohort (n = 110) with and without RBD underwent detailed pain phenotyping without neuroimaging. Participants with iRBD had significantly higher odds of greater pain severity than controls (OR = 2.24, 95%CI 1.17-4.49, p = 0.02). Moderate-severe baseline pain predicted phenoconversion (HR = 2.21, 95%CI 1.13-4.32, p = 0.02), an estimate that remained stable after adjustment for several medical covariates, although the overall three-category model was not statistically significant (p = 0.08). Cross-sectional striatal DAT binding was not associated with symptom severity. Despite greater subjective pain burden, objective pressure algometry did not differ between iRBD and controls. Pain may represent a prodromal symptom of synuclein-based neurodegeneration but was not associated with striatal DAT binding, suggesting that nigrostriatal terminal loss alone does not explain the association.

papers.title: Exploring the genetic determinants of ALS in a North Indian cohort using a genomic screening approach
papers.abstract: Background: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a clinically and genetically heterogenous neurodegenerative disorder in which both monogenic and complex genetic mechanism contribute to disease susceptibility. Increasing evidence also indicates that non motor manifestations, including sleep disturbances, significantly influence disease burden. This study aimed to characterize the genetic spectrum of ALS in a predominantly North Indian cohort while evaluating the prevalence of sleep related abnormalities. Methods: Seventy-three clinically diagnosed ALS patients were recruited from a tertiary care centre in North India. Disease severity was assessed using the ALSFRS-R. Sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, and REM sleep behaviour disorder symptoms were evaluated using the PSQI, ESS and RBDQ questionnaires, respectively. Genetic analysis included targeted sequencing of SOD1, TARDBP, and ANG, followed by repeat expansion analysis of C9orf72, ATXN1, ATXN2, ATXN3, and ATXN7. Whole exome sequencing was performed in selected cases to further investigate the genetic basis of ALS. Results: The cohort demonstrated a male predominance and an earlier age of onset compared to many Western populations. Poor sleep quality and excessive daytime sleepiness were frequently observed although no significant association was found between sleep parameters and disease severity. Genetic screening identified a pathogenic/likely pathogenic TARDBP variant classified by ClinVar while no known or novel pathogenic variants were detected in SOD1 or ANG. Repeat expansion studies revealed one patient harbouring pathogenic C9orf72 repeat expansions. For the ATXN1, one patient harboured pathogenic repeat expansions and two patients carried intermediate length repeats. Additionally, one patient harboured intermediate repeat expansions in ATXN2. Whole exome sequencing revealed novel and rare variants in ALS associated genes including ANXA11, SIGMAR1, SETX, ERBB4 and NEK1, highlighting substantial genetic heterogeneity. Conclusions: Our findings highlight the complex genetic heterogeneity of ALS, with pathogenic repeat expansions and rare variants identified across multiple disease associated genes. These results demonstrate the importance of comprehensive genetic testing to improve the detection of clinically relevant variants in ALS. In addition, the high prevalence of sleep related disturbances observed in the cohort emphasizes the need to incorporate non motor assessment into routine clinical evaluation of patients with ALS.

papers.title: The impact of mindfulness on sleep, cognitive function and athletic performance of young males migrating to the plateau.
papers.abstract: To examine whether an 8-week mindfulness training program was associated with changes in sleep quality, cognitive function, and athletic performance in young men who migrated to high-altitude regions. Ninety-six young male migrants were randomly assigned to an 8-week mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) program (n = 48) or a no-intervention control group (n = 48). Sleep quality (PSQI), cognitive processing (P300 latency), and athletic performance (3000-m run time) were assessed before and after the intervention. The mindfulness group was associated with greater improvements in sleep quality (PSQI median: 7.5 to 5 vs. 8 to 8.5, P < 0.001) and cognitive processing speed (P300 latency median: 387 ms to 357 ms vs. 376.5 ms to 374.5 ms, P = 0.01) compared with controls. Exploratory analyses suggested that P300 amplitude increased in parietal and occipital regions. No significant between-group difference was observed in 3000-m run completion time (P = 0.51) or grade improvement rates (25.0% vs. 29.17%, P = 0.65). An 8-week mindfulness intervention was associated with improved sleep quality and cognitive processing speed, but no significant association was observed with athletic performance, in young male migrants to high-altitude regions. These preliminary findings suggest potential benefits of mindfulness as a non-pharmacological strategy for high-altitude health management, pending replication with active control conditions.

papers.title: Association between sleep bruxism, awake bruxism, perceived stress and coping strategies among dental students: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Bruxism is a common condition that can adversely affect quality of life and may be associated with tooth wear, temporomandibular disorders, and failures of dental restorations. The aim of this cross-sectional study was to investigate whether sleep bruxism (SB) and/or awake bruxism (AB) were associated with perceived stress levels and coping strategies among undergraduate dental students. The study was conducted among undergraduate dental students at Medipol University Faculty of Dentistry, Istanbul, Türkiye. Data were collected using a self-administered questionnaire consisting of demographic information, bruxism-related questions, the 8-item Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), and the 30-item Ways of Coping Inventory (WOCI). Sleep bruxism was assessed using questionnaire items based on the American Academy of Sleep Medicine criteria and a previously published epidemiological study, whereas awake bruxism was determined based on self-reported awareness of clenching or grinding during wakefulness within the previous six months. The PSS and WOCI were administered using their validated Turkish versions. Group comparisons were performed using Student's t-test and chi-square test. Binary logistic regression analyses were conducted to adjust for potential confounding factors. Of the 650 students enrolled during the 2017-2018 academic year, 570 completed the questionnaires. The mean age was 21.08 ± 2.13 years; 58.9% were female and 41.1% were male. The prevalence of sleep bruxism and awake bruxism was 57.4% (n = 327) and 39.5% (n = 225), respectively. Perceived stress levels were significantly higher in participants with sleep bruxism than in those without sleep bruxism (p = 0.011), but did not differ according to awake bruxism status (p = 0.406). Participants with sleep bruxism demonstrated higher emotion-focused, and problem-focused coping scores (all p < 0.05), whereas participants with awake bruxism showed lower problem-focused coping scores than those without awake bruxism (p = 0.018). Multivariable analyses showed that perceived stress (OR=1.034, 95% CI: 1.007-1.062), problem-focused coping (OR=1.024, 95% CI: 1.009-1.039) and emotion-focused coping (OR=1.035, 95% CI: 1.006-1.066) remained independently associated with sleep bruxism. In contrast, only problem-focused coping remained independently associated with awake bruxism (OR=0.984, 95% CI: 0.969-0.998). Within the limitations of this study, sleep bruxism was associated with higher perceived stress levels and greater use of coping strategies, whereas awake bruxism was associated with reduced use of problem-focused coping despite similar perceived stress levels. These findings suggest that sleep bruxism and awake bruxism may have different psychosocial characteristics and should be evaluated separately in future research and clinical practice.

papers.title: Vestibular Epilepsy Presenting With Isolated Recurrent Vertigo and Postictal Headache: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Vestibular epilepsy, also referred to as epileptic vertigo syndrome, is a rare and underrecognized cause of recurrent episodic vertigo. Currently, there are no universally accepted diagnostic criteria for vestibular epilepsy. A 38-year-old woman presented with an eight-month history of recurrent spontaneous episodes of rotational vertigo lasting one to two minutes and occurring multiple times daily. Episodes were accompanied by nausea and vomiting and were followed by bilateral throbbing headaches. Neurological examination, bedside vestibular assessment, and cognitive screening were unremarkable. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated no structural epileptogenic lesion, while brainstem evoked response audiometry was normal. Electroencephalography revealed frequent generalized epileptiform discharges with a photoparoxysmal response during intermittent photic stimulation. The patient was diagnosed with vestibular epilepsy with postictal headache after exclusion of alternative causes of episodic vertigo. Treatment with extended-release divalproex sodium resulted in a marked reduction in attack frequency and improvement in symptoms during follow-up. Vestibular epilepsy represents an uncommon seizure manifestation in which vestibular symptoms predominate and may occur in isolation. In this patient, the brief stereotyped attacks, normal brain neuroimaging, absence of peripheral vestibular abnormalities, epileptiform electroencephalographic findings, and favorable response to antiseizure therapy supported the diagnosis. In cases of recurrent episodic vertigo presenting concurrently with headache, vestibular epilepsy remains a diagnostic challenge, mainly because overt neurological manifestations are often absent. Recent literature suggests that electroencephalography should be considered in patients with recurrent unexplained brief vertigo, particularly when episodes are stereotyped or resistant to conventional vestibular therapies.

papers.title: Success rate of MRI scanning during natural sleep for younger autistic and typically developing toddlers.
papers.abstract: Toddlerhood represents a critical period of brain development in autism, yet there is limited magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data for children ages 1-3 years. These ages are difficult to scan without sedation because toddlers tend to have difficulty falling asleep in noisy, unfamiliar environments and following instructions to stay still. While some studies have successfully scanned typically-developing toddlers without sedation, fewer have scanned autistic toddlers. The few with high success rates (>90%) are not easily replicated (e.g., flexible scan durations). Recent reviews emphasize a need for gold-standard, feasible scan protocols and detailed reporting of natural-sleep methods. To address these gaps, we examined MRI scan success rates and detailed our scanning procedures. Twenty-two autistic and twenty-three typically-developing toddlers attempted scans during natural, non-sedated sleep in our longitudinal study. Our MRI battery included structural, resting-state functional, and diffusion-weighted scans. The overall scan success rate was 40.3%; autism (36.4%) and non-autism groups (44.1%) did not significantly differ. Among unsuccessful scans, 87.5% resulted from toddlers not falling asleep. Success rates did not significantly differ by factors such as age, timepoint, or developmental functioning. While our success rate aligns with most literature describing difficulty scanning 1-3 year-olds, our rate was lower than the few high-rate, natural-sleep studies of autistic toddlers. We identified differences in procedures and budget as key considerations (e.g., absence of standardized pre-visit measures, inability to scan late in evenings). These differences emphasize the need for standardized procedures to bolster success rates and broaden our understanding of early brain development in autism.

papers.title: Occupational exposures and cancer risk associated with the practice of urology: A narrative review.
papers.abstract: Cancer is the leading cause of death (171,630 deaths in 2022), with a rising incidence (433,000 new cases in France in 2023). A recent US study identified cancer as the leading cause of death among surgeons, suggesting an association with occupational constraints and lifestyle. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, covering the period up to April 2026. The selected articles were analyzed qualitatively to identify the various risks to which surgeons are exposed and to assess the position of urology among the surgical specialties evaluated. A total of 98 articles were identified, of which 24 were included. Occupational exposure-related risk factors were identified in the literature. Some are associated with operating-room activity and exposure to known carcinogenic agents, including surgical smoke (containing aromatic hydrocarbons and biological particles), volatile anesthetic agents, and ionizing radiation. Others relate to chronic stress, sleep deprivation, night work, and prolonged working hours. Limited awareness of these risks, inadequate medical follow-up, and potential delays in screening are also reported. Improved awareness of these occupational risks may support the development of preventive strategies for urologic surgeons.

papers.title: Prevalence and Associations of Depressive and Anxiety Symptoms in Age Related Macular Degeneration and Other Macular Diseases.
papers.abstract: Older people with visual impairments are at risk of poor mental health and often do not seek mental health support. This study investigated the prevalence and associations of depression and anxiety in people with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and other macular diseases. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among people with AMD and other macular diseases in Australia. Key outcomes of depression and anxiety were measured using the 15-item Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-15) and the 7-item Generalised Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD-7). Associations between symptoms of depression and anxiety and clinical, demographic and psychosocial variables were explored in multivariable logistic regression analyses, with multiple imputations for missing data. A total of 1364 responses were analysed. The mean age (SD) of the participants was 79.9 years (9.1) and 68.2% were female. Depressive symptoms (GDS-15 > 5) were present in 15.7% and anxiety (GAD-7 > 4) in 20.8% of participants; over half of those with depressive or anxiety symptoms received no mental health support. Fair/worse self-rated vision [adjusted odds ratio: 2.4 (95% confidence interval:1.5-3.9); p < 0.0001], fair/worse self-rated health [2.4 (1.6-3.6); p < 0.001], high falls concern [2.8 (1.5-5.5); p = 0.002], fair/poor sleep quality [1.7 (1.1-2.7); p = 0.02], loneliness [3.3 (2.1-5.1); p < 0.0001], social isolation [2.8 (1.7-4.5); p < 0.0001] and anxiety [6.9 (4.4-10.7); p < 0.0001] were associated with increased odds of depressive symptoms. Older participants (>75 years) had lower odds of anxiety [0.45 (0.3-0.65); p < 0.0001]. High falls concern [2.38 (1.48-3.83); p < 0.0001), fair/worse sleep quality [1.91 (1.35-2.69); p < 0.0001], loneliness [3.54 (2.43-5.15); p < 0.0001] and depressive symptoms [6.14 (3.96-9.53); p < 0.0001] were associated with increased odds of anxiety. Depressive and anxiety symptoms among older adults with macular disease are both associated with loneliness, high falls concern and poor sleep quality. The multifactorial nature of mental health outcomes highlights the need for holistic, patient-centred care that incorporates mental health screening and appropriate referral pathways.

papers.title: Development of a multidimensional scale for discomfort related to personal protective equipment and its exploratory association with musculoskeletal symptoms among Korean healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic.
papers.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic required healthcare workers (HCWs) to use personal protective equipment (PPE) for prolonged periods, raising concerns about its possible relationship with musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs). PPE-related discomfort, however, is multidimensional, encompassing both direct wearing burden and organisational aspects of its deployment. How these two dimensions relate to MSDs has rarely been examined. This cross-sectional study analysed 565 Korean physicians, nurses and medical technicians who had directly cared for patients with COVID-19. A 17-item PPE Discomfort Scale was developed and its factor structure was examined using exploratory factor analysis with oblique rotation. As an exploratory objective, cross-sectional associations between PPE-related discomfort and MSDs were examined using hierarchical modified Poisson regression, adjusting sequentially for demographic, occupational, ergonomic and psychosocial covariates. Exploratory factor analysis yielded two factors; direct wearing burden (Factor 1) and organisational vulnerability (Factor 2). The prevalence of MSDs was 37.2%, with the lower back most frequently affected (19.5%). Greater total PPE discomfort was associated with MSDs (adjusted prevalence ratio 1.60, 95% CI 1.18-2.16 in the ergonomic-adjusted model). When the two subscales were entered simultaneously, the association was observed for organisational vulnerability (1.48, 95% CI 1.14-1.93), but not for direct wearing burden (0.98, 95% CI 0.67-1.44). Sleep disturbance, traumatic experience, current smoking and ergonomic exposure were independently associated with MSDs. After further adjustment for current smoking, sleep disturbance and traumatic experience, these associations were attenuated and no longer statistically significant (total score 1.28, 95% CI 0.95-1.74; organisational vulnerability 1.25, 95% CI 0.96-1.62), whereas ergonomic exposure remained associated with MSDs. The PPE Discomfort Scale identified two dimensions: direct wearing burden and organisational vulnerability, supporting a multidimensional conceptualisation of PPE-related discomfort. In exploratory analyses, organisational vulnerability showed a stronger association with MSDs, although this association was attenuated after additional adjustment. Further studies are needed to confirm the factor structure and evaluate the scale in other healthcare settings.
